Body mass index in adults aged 30 and over in Bharatpur, Nepal

Dataset 4: Nepal hypertension and cardiovascular risk-factor survey

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

This is a community-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged 30 years and over living in Bharatpur, Chitwan district, Nepal, run to estimate the prevalence of hypertension and its cardiovascular risk factors (Dhungana and colleagues, PLOS ONE 2016, e0185806). Height and weight were measured directly by trained enumerators rather than self-reported, and the WHO STEPS instrument supplied the behavioural and socio-economic information. Body mass index is worth analysing in its own right in this setting: Nepal is in the middle of a nutrition transition in which under- and over-nutrition coexist in the same communities, and the classical Western socio-economic gradient in adiposity (poorer people heavier) is often reversed in South Asia.

Aim. Among adults aged 30 and over in Bharatpur, we examined which of sex, age band, education, occupation, poverty, smoking, smokeless tobacco, alcohol, fruit and vegetable intake, salt intake, physical activity and family history of hypertension are independently associated with body mass index, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional survey of 1159 adults aged 30 years and over resident in Bharatpur Municipality, Chitwan, Nepal. The source study used multistage cluster sampling: four wards were selected at random and roughly 300 participants enrolled in each, with the sample size calculation assuming a design effect of 1.5. The ward identifier is not present in this extract (see Limitations). Each row is one participant.

Variables. The outcome is bmi, measured body mass index in kg/m2. Predictors are sex (reference Female); age band in years (reference 30-39; age was recorded only in four bands, so a per-year effect cannot be estimated); education (reference None or informal); main occupation (reference Household work); family income per head below the poverty line (reference No); smoking status (reference Never); current smokeless tobacco use (reference No); any alcohol in the last month (reference No); fruit and vegetable servings per day; estimated salt intake in g/day; physical activity level (reference Moderate or high); and family history of hypertension (reference No).

Because body mass index is the outcome here it is of course not also a predictor, and – less obviously – neither are systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, hypertension, bp_awareness or antihypertensive_drug. Adiposity raises blood pressure, so blood pressure is a consequence of the outcome; conditioning on it would be adjusting for a mediator of everything upstream and would bias every remaining coefficient. This is the mirror image of the systolic and diastolic analyses in this catalogue, where bmi is a legitimate predictor. Two further pairs of variables measure the same construct twice and only one of each may enter a model: physical_activity is a deterministic cut of mets_min_per_week at 600 MET-minutes per week (the “Low” group spans 0-600 and “Moderate or high” spans 620-29,260), and the categorical version is used here because it is the WHO STEPS classification the source paper reports and because the continuous version is extremely right-skewed; and cigarettes_per_week is zero for every never-smoker, so smoking_status is used instead because it also separates former from never smokers.

Statistical analysis. Linear regression via lm(), justified because the outcome is continuous. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model() and performance::check_heteroscedasticity(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 1159 of 1159 rows were analysed (0 dropped). Every variable in this file is 100% complete, so listwise deletion removes no rows at all and there is no missing-data story: no imputation, no complete-case selection bias.

Mean body mass index was 23.8 kg/m2 (SD 4.2), with a mildly right-skewed distribution running from 13.4 to 41.7 kg/m2. Using the WHO Asian action points, 55.3% of the sample is at or above 23 kg/m2 and 17.9% at or above 27.5 kg/m2, while 9.2% are below 18.5 kg/m2 – the coexistence of under- and over-nutrition that characterises the Nepali nutrition transition. The sample is 71.1% female, a consequence of daytime household recruitment in the source survey.

Exploratory figure

Figure 3. Body mass index by age band and sex. Dashed lines mark the WHO Asian action points of 23 and 27.5 kg/m2.

Body mass index is remarkably flat across the age bands until the oldest group, where it drops by about a kilogram per square metre in both sexes, and women sit slightly above men at every age – so unlike blood pressure, adiposity in this population is not primarily an age story.

The crude associations are all small. The largest is family history of hypertension, whose presence is associated with a 1.41 kg/m2 higher body mass index (95% CI 0.72 to 2.09, p <0.001) – plausible, since familial hypertension and familial adiposity share both genes and household food environment. Current smoking is associated with a -1.58 kg/m2 lower BMI (95% CI -2.22 to -0.94), and smokeless tobacco with -1.4 kg/m2 (95% CI -2.14 to -0.66), both familiar findings. Poverty is associated with -0.97 kg/m2 (95% CI -1.51 to -0.42) – the South Asian direction, in which the poor are thinner, the opposite of the high-income-country gradient. Men average -0.84 kg/m2 below women, and the oldest band averages -1.44 kg/m2 below the 30-39 band. Salt intake is flat (-0.036 kg/m2 per g/day) and, notably, so is low physical activity (0.043 kg/m2, 95% CI -0.46 to 0.55, p = 0.87), which is not what one would predict and is the first sign that the behavioural variables in this file carry little information about adiposity.

Why adjustment is needed

The crude estimates above are entangled through two variables in particular. Sex is the main one, because every tobacco and alcohol variable in this dataset is strongly sex-patterned while sex is itself associated with BMI: 35% of men are current smokers against 11% of women, and 39% of men drank in the last month against 6% of women, while men average 0.84 kg/m2 less than women. A crude “smoking lowers BMI” coefficient therefore contains a large “being male lowers BMI” component. Occupation is the second, and it is confounded with sex in an extreme way in this sample: 595 of the 659 people doing household work are women, whereas paid employment is 53% male. Occupation is also a proxy for both physical exertion at work and household income, both of which act on BMI. Age band plays a third, smaller role: BMI falls in the oldest band while smoking cessation, low education and low physical activity all rise with age, so crude coefficients for those variables absorb some of the age-related weight loss. Mutual adjustment is needed to tell these apart.

The model explains 8% of the variance in body mass index (adjusted R-squared 0.064), so more than 90% of the variation between these adults is unexplained by twelve socio-demographic and behavioural characteristics. That is the headline result and it is a real one, not a technical failure: this predictor set simply does not contain the determinants of adiposity. There are 1159 observations for 20 parameters (58 per parameter), so the weak fit is not an overfitting artefact.

Conditional on the other eleven predictors, family history of hypertension remains the largest effect at 1.35 kg/m2 (95% CI 0.68 to 2.02, p <0.001). Current smokers average -1.01 kg/m2 below never-smokers (95% CI -1.75 to -0.28), smokeless tobacco users -0.94 kg/m2 below non-users (95% CI -1.81 to -0.08), and people below the poverty line -0.65 kg/m2 below those above it (95% CI -1.2 to -0.1). Participants in paid employment or self-employment average 0.88 kg/m2 above those doing household work (95% CI 0.24 to 1.53), and the oldest band -1.1 kg/m2 below the youngest (95% CI -1.85 to -0.34). Every one of these is under one and a half kg/m2 – roughly 4 kg for an adult of average height – so even the “significant” findings are modest.

Physical activity is the striking null: low activity is associated with 0.35 kg/m2 (95% CI -0.15 to 0.86, p = 0.17), pointing in the wrong direction of nothing at all. Salt (-0.064 kg/m2 per g/day) and education (all categories p > 0.2) are equally flat.

Three predictors move meaningfully and all three move toward the null. Sex goes from -0.84 kg/m2 crude (95% CI -1.38 to -0.31, p = 0.002) to -0.56 kg/m2 adjusted (95% CI -1.26 to 0.14, p = 0.12) and loses significance: about a third of the crude male–female difference in BMI is really the fact that men smoke, chew tobacco and work outside the home. Smokeless tobacco shrinks from -1.4 to -0.94 kg/m2, a 33% reduction, and only just keeps significance (p = 0.032), for the same reason. Fruit and vegetable servings moves from 0.272 kg/m2 per serving crude (p = 0.006) to 0.169 adjusted (p = 0.09), crossing from significant to not. Occupation in agriculture or labour likewise falls from -1.12 kg/m2 (p = 0.004) to -0.57 (p = 0.17), confirming that the crude occupational gradient was mostly sex.

One predictor flips sign. Alcohol in the last month is -0.38 kg/m2 crude (95% CI -1.06 to 0.3, p = 0.27) but 0.67 kg/m2 adjusted (95% CI -0.12 to 1.45, p = 0.09) – neither estimate significant, but the direction reverses because drinkers are overwhelmingly male and men are lighter; once sex is held fixed, alcohol’s own calorie contribution shows through. This is textbook negative confounding, and worth pointing out precisely because neither estimate is significant: sign changes are not confined to significant coefficients.

Two predictors barely move. Family history of hypertension goes from 1.41 to 1.35 kg/m2 (a shift of under 5%) and stays highly significant, which is what one expects of a variable essentially unrelated to the others in the model. Low physical activity goes from 0.043 to 0.355 kg/m2 and is null throughout. The maximum variance inflation factor is 1.82, so none of these movements reflect collinearity; they are confounding by sex, occupation and age.

Diagnostics

The homogeneity of variance panel is the one that matters most for a linear model and here it passes: check_heteroscedasticity() returns p = 0.102, so constant error variance is a defensible assumption and robust standard errors are not required. They are shown above anyway for comparison and, as expected when the assumption holds, they are almost identical to the ordinary ones. The posterior-predictive check shows the model tracking the centre of the BMI distribution while under-predicting the right tail, because BMI is right-skewed and a linear model with additive terms generates a symmetric predictive distribution; the normality of residuals panel says the same thing, with a clear upward departure in the upper QQ tail (check_normality() flags it at p < 0.001). Neither is a serious threat with 1159 observations, but it does mean prediction intervals for individuals would be wrong even though the coefficient estimates are fine. The linearity panel is flat. Collinearity is unproblematic despite the strong sex–occupation association: maximum VIF 1.82. Influential observations shows the handful of participants with BMI above 40 approaching but not crossing the Cook’s distance contour. The real diagnostic problem is not in these panels at all: it is that adjusted R-squared is 0.064, so the model is a poor description of adiposity whatever its assumptions.

Discussion

Body mass index in these Bharatpur adults is barely predicted by the socio-demographic and behavioural variables collected in a STEPS survey. The associations that survive adjustment are all small and mostly point the way South Asian nutrition-transition literature would predict: people below the poverty line are lighter, not heavier (-0.65 kg/m2); tobacco users of both kinds are lighter; people in paid employment are heavier than those doing household work; and BMI declines in the oldest band. Family history of hypertension carries the largest single association at 1.35 kg/m2, consistent with shared familial and household determinants of cardiometabolic risk. Physical activity, salt, fruit and vegetables and education are all null. In practical terms, the message is that adiposity in this population is not readily explained by, or targeted through, the behaviours this instrument measures.

Limitations. The dominant limitation is the weak model: adjusted R-squared 0.064 means that essentially nothing here explains BMI, and the most important determinants – total energy intake, dietary composition beyond fruit and vegetable servings, sedentary time, parity and menopausal status in women, genetics – are simply not measured. Second, the cluster sampling cannot be accounted for: only four wards were randomly selected with around 300 participants each and a design effect of 1.5 assumed in the sample size calculation, but this extract contains no ward identifier, so all confidence intervals above are too narrow (plausibly by around 20%) and cannot be corrected. Estimates from four clusters cannot be generalised to Nepal or even to all of Bharatpur. Third, age is available only in four bands, so no per-year change in BMI can be estimated and the top band is open-ended. Fourth, this is cross-sectional, so the smoking and tobacco coefficients cannot be read causally: low body weight may lead to continued smoking as much as the reverse, and people who gain weight may quit. Fifth, physical_activity is a crude binary derived from a self-reported MET score with well-known over-reporting problems, which may explain its complete lack of association. Sixth, BMI itself does not distinguish fat from lean mass and performs poorly in South Asian populations, where cardiometabolic risk begins at lower BMI values – waist circumference would have been a better outcome but is not in this extract. On the credit side, the file has no missing data at all (all 1159 rows complete on all 21 variables), and height and weight were measured rather than self-reported, so the outcome itself is of good quality.

Future work. Repeat with waist circumference or waist-to-height ratio as the outcome, add dietary energy intake and sedentary time, and refit with the ward identifier as a random effect.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Technically clean but substantively thin. Complete data, a well-behaved continuous outcome, homoscedastic residuals (p = 0.102), maximum VIF 1.82, 1159 rows over 20 parameters. The problem is that adjusted R-squared is 0.064 – this predictor set does not explain BMI.
  • Set expectations in the brief. A student who equates a good report with a high R-squared will conclude they have done something wrong. The teaching value is the opposite: this is what an honest, well-conducted, largely null Purpose 3 analysis looks like.
  • BMI is a predictor in the other files in this dataset and the outcome here. It must be dropped from the predictor set in this file, and blood pressure (systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, hypertension, bp_awareness, antihypertensive_drug) must not be added as predictors: BP is downstream of adiposity, so conditioning on it adjusts away the very pathway of interest. This is the single most likely student error in this file, and it is seductive because adding systolic BP would roughly triple R-squared.
  • Deterministic twins. physical_activity is exactly mets_min_per_week <= 600; cigarettes_per_week is zero for all never-smokers. Never both.
  • The interesting stories are counter-intuitive. Poverty is associated with lower BMI, and physical activity with nothing at all. Both are correct for this setting but will read as errors to students trained on Western data, so they need framing.
  • One genuine sign flip (alcohol, -0.38 crude to 0.67 adjusted) makes this a good file for teaching negative confounding, though neither estimate is significant.
  • No ward identifier, so the assumed design effect of 1.5 cannot be honoured; standard errors are too narrow throughout.
  • Age in bands only, so no per-year BMI trajectory is estimable.
  • Residual non-normality from the right tail of BMI is flagged and will worry students unnecessarily; it does not threaten the coefficients at this sample size.
